To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose a novel affordances dataset, and a new method to predict affordances from images that exploits Graph Neural Network to reason over scene context.

(i) we introduce a novel dataset, ADE-Aff, which contains affordance labels for 150k images; (ii) we show how to predict affordances for each object, and how to reason about the consequences of taking actions on them, by exploiting a Graph Neural Network architecture; (iii) we show how our model can be used to teach artificial agents about the consequences of their actions.

we: 1) collect a new dataset, ADE-Aff, that enables affordance reasoning in the real world; 2) develop a model that predicts and explains affordances from egocentric images; 3) perform a series of experiments that showcase the model’s successes and challenges.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how an agent should act in a given scene.
the question: how can we predict the affordances of the objects in a scene, and why are these affordances valid or not?
understanding the physical and social world through affordances, in order to teach artificial agents how to act properly in the real world.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed model is able to perform a rich affordance reasoning in complex scenes, but it still struggles to learn the social rules imposed by the society, and it is unable to reason about the consequences of the actions.

our work is a step towards a better understanding of how affordances are perceived in complex real-world environments, and how this knowledge can be exploited to enable agents to reason about actions and their consequences.
the proposed model is able to learn to reason about affordances from images, but there are still a lot of open challenges to be addressed in order to achieve more robust performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our model is able to predict affordances in diverse scenes, and can explain its reasoning in the form of an affordance graph.
we are the first to tackle the problem of affordances reasoning in the wild and to provide a dataset for that.
we show that it is feasible to predict action-object affordances in real scenes, and that the predictions are explainable and interpretable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
affordance reasoning is a promising direction for the future development of artificial agents, and we hope that the dataset we release will be a valuable resource for the community.
we show that it is indeed possible to learn affordances from images and use these to predict and explain what should and should not be done in different situations.

the proposed model can be successfully used for affordance prediction in diverse scenes, as well as for teaching artificial agents about the social norms that should be followed in these scenes.
